newsitem.title: FRANCE: No sign of let-up in the agony of Algeria.
newsitem.headline: No sign of let-up in the agony of Algeria.

text.p: The agony of Algeria, its mountain villages and isolated hamlets awash with blood, shows no sign of easing.
Moslem fundamentalist rebels and security forces are dug in for a long struggle in which civilians will as usual be the main casualties, political analysts and diplomats said on Sunday.
"The latest killings are part of the same grind. The violence has its peaks and valleys and a middle zone. It's going to go on for years," said one Western diplomat in the Algerian capital.

More than 170 villagers were slaughtered in the past week in hill villages near Algiers and on the Mitidja plain. A car bomb killed eight people in Algiers and five policemen died in ambushes in the capital, Algerian newspapers said.
At the weekend, the influential El Watan newspaper said the violence gave "an impression of a return to square one of the first years of terrorism in Algeria".
Between 500 and 600 civilians have died since Algeria's June 5 general election, held to fill the void caused by the cancellation in 1992 of one in which Islamists had taken a huge lead.

The violence that erupted after the voiding of the vote in 1992 started with the killing of mostly security forces, then stepped up to male civilians. Women, children and babies later joined the bloody toll, which has swollen to about 60,000 dead.
The killers, who started with gunfire and bombs, increasingly turned to throat-cutting, beheading and even the disembowelling of pregnant women. Some victims lately have been burned alive.

"The massacres are horrible but they are not new," said the Western diplomat. "They have been going on for a year. There are fewer car bombs than a couple of years ago. I don't think we are back to 'square one'."

A European analyst said he thought a long-term conflict was inevitable, and this could pose its own dangers: "Unless the authorities can get the economy right for ordinary people -- do something about the shortage of housing, get jobs -- there's a danger that the rebels can get more popular support."
Another Western analyst echoed this: "Clearly the terrorists have some element of sympathy in the population. They obviously have a network.
"What is not clear is whether massacres affect this political support. You would expect them to, but it's impossible to say."

Officials blame Moslem rebels for the killings. At first the killers were described as hardliners of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) who took to the gun after the party was thwarted of election victory by the 1992 vote-scrapping, and later outlawed.

Then came other factions, with the Armed Islamic Group (GIA) seen as the most ruthless. No one knows how much sway, if any, FIS political leaders such as Abassi Madani, recently freed early from a 12-year jail term, have over the armed rebels.

Besides the desire of most of the country's 29 million people to live in peace, the authorities have a militant support network. Many villages have their "Patriots" -- volunteer groups armed by the government, to defend their community.

But some of these volunteer vigilantes want more action from the government, at least to make the villages they are defending better places to live in. Last week, El Watan cited the anger and frustration of several Patriot members.
"Since we set up as Patriots, terrorists no longer take the risk of coming into our village..," said one young man, proud of his group's ability to defend the community.
But he said: "Today, the authorities must think of resurrecting our village from the cinders. We have neither electricity, water, nor gas. Public lighting doesn't exist."
Another asked: "Do you think you can fight terrorism only with weapons? The best way to fight the enemies of God is to rebuild what has been destroyed."

On the other side of this merciless conflict, security forces have killed more than 300 rebels, newspapers say. Most of these killings go unreported officially. There is silence, or statements that "terrorism" is being defeated.
After the car bomb last week, Le Matin newspaper criticised what it termed "triumphalist speeches". "If terrorism has been conquered politicaly, it has still to be fought on the ground," it said.
Algeria holds local elections on October 23 in what is seen as the first test of support for the new three-party government coalition, dominated by supporters of President Liamine Zeroual.
Those elected to run town halls face a tough challenge.

"It is above all in isolated communities that you find the real Algeria. The terrorists know this. That is why they attack peaceful citizens with an unimaginable violence," said Patriot member Abdelkader in one village on the Mitidja plain.

"If today I am angry, it is because we do not merit the hard life we lead. We are not asking (the authorities) for the moon. Just a minimum to live decently, a salary to be able to feed our families and the means to eradicate all the terrorists once and for all. We want also our children to be able to go to school."
